You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly present its content as a drawing rather than as a photograph with blur or texture overlays?
node.criteria: pass: substantial depicted content has clearly drawn or illustrated rendering, not merely softened contours or texture over photographic detail; fail: the content remains clearly photographic without a genuine drawing conversion; unknown: evidence does not reliably distinguish a drawing from filtered photographic detail.
node.binding: Assess only drawing-versus-photographic rendering. Do not assess chalk medium; do not treat blur, grain, or softened contours alone as proof of a drawing.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image renders the giraffes and surroundings with visibly illustrated, sketch-like contours and simplified shading rather than retaining the source photograph’s detailed photographic appearance. This supports a drawing conversion; chalk medium is not assessed here.
The edited image retains photographic detail and recognizable photo-like giraffes and scenery, with blur and grainy texture overlays rather than a clearly drawn or illustrated rendering.

The edited image renders the giraffes and surroundings with visibly illustrated, sketch-like contours and simplified, painterly forms rather than retaining clear photographic detail. This supports a drawing conversion; the chalk medium is not assessed here.

The edited image retains photographic detail and recognizable photo-like giraffe and landscape rendering, with blur and grain-like texture overlays rather than a clearly drawn or illustrated conversion.

The edited image renders the giraffes and surroundings with visibly illustrated, hand-drawn contours and shading rather than retaining photographic detail with only blur or texture. This assesses drawing conversion only, not whether the medium is chalk.

n3: The node’s binding is too underspecified: it asks whether the image became a chalk drawing but does not make the two distinct requirements and the partial-progress rule operational. Clarify that the saved supports must be combined without treating a chalk-like texture alone as proof of drawing conversion, or a drawing-like rendering alone as proof of chalk medium. In particular, when one support affirms chalk-like treatment and the other reports retained photographic detail/no clear drawing conversion, preserve that affirmative progress as partial; do not promote it to complete merely because both cues are described positively elsewhere. The traces vary between complete and partial on similar support evidence, suggesting the criterion needs a stable distinction between genuine scene-wide drawing conversion and surface effects over photo-like content.
